title: Window with a counter
sub: A replacement budget, a maxFreq you never decrease, and Minimum Window Substring with a “how many still needed” counter
cards/0/title: The problem: a window with a replacement budget
cards/0/body:
Longest Repeating Character Replacement (LeetCode #424). Given a string s of uppercase English letters and a number k, you may replace at most k characters with any uppercase letters. Find the length of the longest substring of one repeated letter you can get this way. Constraints: 1 ≤ |s| ≤ 10⁵, 0 ≤ k ≤ |s|.

Example: "AABABBA", k = 1 → 4: in “AABA” replace the B with an A.

Rephrase it. Which letter do you keep in a window? The most frequent one — everything else has to be replaced. So a window is valid when

length − maxFreq ≤ k, where maxFreq is how many times the most frequent letter occurs in the window.

The condition is monotonic: remove a character from a valid window and the length drops by 1 while maxFreq drops by at most 1, so “length − maxFreq” does not grow. That means the variable-size window from the previous lesson works, and the letter frequencies of the window live in an int[26] counter: a letter enters — count[c − 'A']++, it leaves — --.
cards/1/explain: “AABBA”: length 5, the most frequent is A ×3, replace 5 − 3 = 2 ≤ 2 — valid, it becomes “AAAAA”. In “ABCAB” the most frequent are A and B with 2 each: replace 3 > 2. In “ABCDA” A ×2: replace 3 > 2.
cards/1/wrong/1: The most frequent letters, A and B, occur twice each. Keep one of them and you replace 5 − 2 = 3 characters, with a budget of 2.
cards/1/wrong/2: A occurs twice, the others once: replace 5 − 2 = 3 > 2.
cards/2/title: The honest version: a while and the true maximum
cards/2/body:
The “longest” template from the previous lesson: add s[r], shrink from the left while the window is bad, then update the answer. Bad means more than k replacements are needed: r − l + 1 − maxFreq > k.

Here maxFreq is recomputed every time over 26 counters. A step costs O(26), the pass — O(26·n), which is O(n) with a constant of 26. Memory is O(26).

Invariant: after the while the window is valid — at most k letters need replacing.

count.Max() is LINQ: in Unity it also allocates an enumerator on every call. In a hot loop write your own loop over the 26 slots, but in an interview this form reads better. And below is how to get rid of those 26 operations too.
cards/3/task: Step through the trace on "AABABBA", k = 1. The rig stops twice when the window turns bad and asks what the honest version does.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Removes the “A” on the left: l = 1
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Removes the “B” it has just added
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: Window “AABAB”: length 5, the most frequent is A ×3, 2 replacements needed > 1. What does the code do?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: The window is bad, so the while runs: remove the leftmost “A”, l = 1. The answer is only updated after the while, once the window is valid again — best = 5 cannot be recorded. And the window never shrinks on the right: r only grows.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Removes another “A” on the left: window “BAB”
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Stops shrinking and adds the next “B”
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: The “A” is gone: window “ABAB”, length 4, the most frequent is now ×2, 2 replacements. What next?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: 4 − 2 = 2 > 1 — the window is still bad, and the while removes the next “A”: “BAB”, 1 replacement. Notice: the honest version recomputed the maximum from 3 down to 2 and so shrank the window to length 3, below the record of 4. The next card shows a version that does not do that.
cards/4/title: Why maxFreq never needs to go down
cards/4/body:
We don’t need every valid window, only a window longer than the record. A window of length L is valid when L − maxFreq ≤ k, that is L ≤ maxFreq + k. So the record can only grow when maxFreq grows — the highest letter frequency we have ever seen in a window.

Hence the classic solution:
— update maxFreq upwards only: maxFreq = Math.Max(maxFreq, ++count[c]) — only the letter that has just entered needs checking;
— if the window turned bad, move l once: if instead of while. The window does not shrink, it slides to the right, keeping the length of the record.

While maxFreq is stale — too high — the window may in fact be invalid. But a window of that length was already found honestly, so the answer is not spoiled. The window can only grow when the counter of the incoming letter exceeds the old maxFreq, and that is a real frequency in the current window.

Invariant: the window length equals the best answer so far, and the window never gets shorter. That is why you can return s.Length − l at the end. The time is an honest O(n), memory O(26).
cards/5/q: The version with an if and a maxFreq that never decreases. "AABABBA", k = 1. At r = 4 the window “AABAB” is bad: 5 − 3 = 2 > 1. What happens next?
cards/5/options/0: l moves by one, and the window “ABAB” of length 4 with the stale maxFreq = 3 counts as valid
cards/5/options/1: l keeps moving until the window is honestly valid: “BAB”
cards/5/options/2: maxFreq is recomputed down to 2, and the window shrinks to “BAB”
cards/5/explain: The if moves l exactly once, maxFreq stays 3, so 4 − 3 = 1 ≤ 1 — the window “ABAB” counts as valid, even though honestly it needs 2 replacements. The answer is not spoiled: length 4 was already achieved by the honest window “AABA” at r = 3. The window simply slides at length 4 and grows only if some letter reaches frequency 4.
cards/5/wrong/1: That is what the honest version with a while does. In the if version the window never shrinks below the record; it moves by one.
cards/5/wrong/2: maxFreq is only updated through Math.Max, that is, only upwards. That is exactly why no recount over 26 counters is needed.
cards/6/title: Minimum Window Substring: a “how many still needed” counter
cards/6/body:
Minimum Window Substring (LeetCode #76, hard). Given strings s and t, find the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t including repeats, or the empty string. Constraints: 1 ≤ |s|, |t| ≤ 10⁵, uppercase and lowercase English letters. Follow-up: O(|s| + |t|).

Example: s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" → “BANC”.

We want the shortest, so it is the “shrink while the window is good, answer inside the while” template. The question is how to tell quickly that the window is good. Comparing the window’s dictionary with that of t at every step is O(σ) per step.

Instead, keep two counters: need[c] — how many c are needed, have[c] — how many are in the window. Plus a number formed — how many distinct letters of t are already fully covered. The window covers t ⇔ formed == need.Count, and need.Count − formed is how many letters are still missing.

The key: formed changes only at the moment of crossing. You add c and have[c] becomes exactly need[c] — the letter is covered, formed++. You remove c and have[c] drops below need[c] — it is uncovered, formed--. Extra copies change nothing. The check is O(1), the whole pass is O(|s| + |t|).
cards/6/deep:
One counter instead of formed. The classic short version: missing = t.Length — how many characters are still missing, repeats included. c enters: if need[c] > 0, then missing--; then need[c]-- (a negative value means surplus). c leaves: need[c]++; if it became > 0, then missing++. The window covers t ⇔ missing == 0. One array instead of two dictionaries.

Arrays instead of dictionaries. The letters are English, so an int[128] indexed by character code is several times faster than a Dictionary<char, int>: no hashing, no TryGetValue. Span<int> need = stackalloc int[128] removes the allocation too. GetValueOrDefault on a dictionary is an extension method from CollectionExtensions: available since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity since 2021.2.

A filtered string. If t is short and s is full of irrelevant letters, you can first collect a list of (index, character) pairs for the letters of t only and run the window over it: fewer steps, and the window length is computed from the original indices. Same asymptotics.

One allocation. Call Substring once, at the end: keep only bestL and bestLen. Allocating a string on every new record is needless garbage.
cards/7/explain: formed counts distinct letters, so compare it with need.Count, not t.Length: for t = "AABC" there are three letters but the length is four. The leaving character is the left one, s[l++]. A letter becomes uncovered when there are fewer than needed: have[gone] < m; with <= an extra copy would wrongly decrease formed. .NET Substring takes a start and a length, not a start and an end.
cards/8/task: Step through the trace on s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC". The rig stops in the middle of a long shrink and asks what happens when a needed letter is on the left.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: “CODEBA” is no shorter than “ADOBEC”; the “C” is dropped and coverage is lost
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: “CODEBA” is the new best window; the “C” is dropped
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Shrinking stops: the “C” is needed and cannot be dropped
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: The window “CODEBA” covers t, and a “C” is on the left. The best so far is “ADOBEC”. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: The lengths are equal, 6 and 6, and the record is only updated when r − l + 1 < bestLen — strictly less. Then the code drops the “C” like any left character: it cannot look ahead. have[C] falls to 0 < 1, formed = 2, and the while ends. Then the window grows to the next “C” and finds “BANC”.
cards/9/q: On s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" this code returns "BA" instead of "BANC". Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: formed must change only at the moment have[c] crosses need[c]. With >= every extra copy of an already covered letter increases formed again: a second B or A counts as one more covered letter, formed reaches need.Count without a C, and the code declares “BA” a cover. It must be == n: a letter gets covered exactly once.
cards/10/title: Variations: the same counter in other problems
cards/10/body:
A permutation inside a string (Permutation in String #567, Find All Anagrams #438). A fixed-size window of length |p| and letter counters: a letter enters — ++, leaves — --. A match is detected not by comparing 26 slots but with the same formed: how many letters match in count.

At most K distinct (Fruit Into Baskets #904 is K = 2). A variable-size window with a Dictionary<int, int> counter; when a value’s count drops to zero, remove the key — then cnt.Count is the number of distinct values. Shrink while there are more than K.

Exactly K distinct (Subarrays with K Different Integers #992, hard). “Exactly” is not monotonic: removing an element can move you away from K in either direction. The trick: exactly(K) = atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1). And “atMost” counts the number of subarrays: if the window [l..r] is valid, so are all windows that end at r and start no further left than l — there are r − l + 1 of them. Add that number at every step.
cards/10/deep:
Overflowing the count. There are n(n + 1)/2 subarrays: for n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ — more than int.MaxValue. In #992 n ≤ 2·10⁴ and an int is enough, but in your own problem or a similar one with a larger n count in long — interviewers often check exactly that.

Why the difference is right. The set of subarrays with at most K distinct values is the union of those with exactly K and those with at most K − 1, and the two do not overlap. Both “at most” conditions are monotonic, so each is counted by a window in O(n), and the whole problem is O(n).

Counting by key without a double lookup. cnt[x] = cnt.GetValueOrDefault(x) + 1 looks the key up twice. .NET 6+ has CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(cnt, x, out _)++ — one lookup and a reference to the value. Unity does not have it; if the keys are small numbers, a counter array is faster anyway.
cards/11/q: Match each problem with its technique.
cards/11/pairs/0/0: Does s contain a permutation of p
cards/11/pairs/0/1: A window of length |p| and letter counters
cards/11/pairs/1/0: The longest block given k replacements
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Length − maxFreq ≤ k, maxFreq upwards only
cards/11/pairs/2/0: The shortest window with all letters of t
cards/11/pairs/3/0: The number of subarrays with exactly k distinct
cards/11/pairs/4/0: The longest subarray with at most 2 distinct
cards/11/pairs/4/1: Count distinct, shrink while there are more than 2
cards/12/q: You are solving Minimum Window Substring out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: repeats in t count, case matters, what to return if there is no window
cards/12/items/1: Name the brute force: from every start grow until t is covered — O(|s|²), too slow for 10⁵
cards/12/items/2: Idea: a “shortest” window — grow until it covers t, then shrink while it still covers
cards/12/items/3: Counters need and have, and formed — how many letters are covered; it changes only when crossing need[c]
cards/12/items/4: Run ADOBECODEBANC / ABC and show where the window loses coverage
cards/12/items/5: State the complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time, O(σ) memory
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: |t| > |s|, a letter of t missing from s, repeats in t such as "AA"
cards/12/explain: First agree on repeats and case — they change the solution. Then the baseline, the window idea, the key trick — formed instead of comparing dictionaries — a run, the complexity and edge cases. Repeats in t are the main source of bugs, so check them out loud.
